title: Volozhin
hookLine: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin founds a new kind of yeshiva

lines: A HALL THAT SOUNDS LIKE A MARKET.
cards: A long wooden table. Two young men bent over one open book, both talking at once. One reads a line aloud in a singsong.
The other shakes his head: no, that can't be what it means, look at the next word. They argue, they laugh, they go back to the line. Down the table, pair after pair is doing the same.
It sounds more like a market than a library. Someone passing the door might think a fight had broken out. It hasn't.
This is serious study, in a hall in a small town called Volozhin.

teach.h: A STUDENT OF THE VILNA GAON.
teach.b: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin had been a student of the Vilna Gaon. He took his teacher's love of study and gave it a building.

Histories remember it as a new kind of academy: one that gathered students from many places, who left home to live and learn there, supported by gifts from Jewish communities far beyond Volozhin itself.
In a sense, it belonged to everyone who paid for it. Tradition says the sound of learning in its hall was meant never to stop, day or night, with students taking turns. Why did that matter?

teach.h: STUDY THAT HELPS HOLD THE WORLD.
teach.b: In his book Nefesh HaChaim, Chaim teaches that Torah study is not only good for the person studying; it helps hold the whole world in being.
Seen that way, a hall where learning never stops is a kind of watch kept for the world. And notice how the learning happens: in pairs, out loud, arguing.
Proverbs has a line for it, in the King James wording: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend."
The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, reads that verse about two students of Torah, who sharpen each other like two blades.
In the same passage a rabbi says he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and most of all from his students.
That is the idea of the yeshiva: you learn Torah across a table, from someone who refuses to let your first answer stand.

how: In yeshivas today, students commonly study Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating each line, in a shared hall called the beit midrash.

games.q: you are Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin, and you want to build a place of Torah study. how do you set it up?
o: the town pays for it, and it serves the town's own sons.
students come from many places, and communities far away help support it.
each student studies alone, in silence, in his own room.
games.why: he gathered students from many places, supported beyond his own town, learning aloud and, tradition says, without stopping.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has sharpened you: a friend who argued back, a coworker who asked the question you missed, a child who asked why.
Picture the two of you at a table with something open between you, and ask what they showed you that you couldn't see alone.
